ISSUE
Adopt Resolution No. SA 2021-001 approving the Recognized Obligation Payment
Schedule (ROPS 21-22) for the period of July 1, 2021 through June 30, 2022 and;

Adopt Resolution No. SA 2021-002 approving the Administrative Budget for the Period
of July 1, 2021 through June 30, 2022 (Administrative Budget 21-22)

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Adopt Resolution No. SA 2021-001 approving the Recognized Obligation
  Payment Schedule (ROPS 21-22) for the period of July 1, 2021 through June 30,
  2022

  2. Adopt Resolution No. SA 2021-002 approving the Administrative Budget for the
  Period of July 1, 2021 through June 30, 2022 (Administrative Budget 21-22)

BACKGROUND
As part of the wind down of Redevelopment Agencies, the State requires Successor
Agencies to submit an approved Recognized Obligation Payment Schedule and a
proposed administrative budget annually. This requires approval by both the City and the
Oversight Board prior to submission to the State Department of Finance.

DISCUSSION
The total payments estimated during the one year period of ROPS 21-22 is $17,865,272,
of which $10,840,324 is expected to be funded by Redevelopment Property Tax Trust
Funds (RPTTF) to be received from the Los Angeles County Auditor Controller
(including Administrative Cost Allowance), $6,576,324 is from reserve balance funds,
and $448,624 is from other funds. Amounts are budgeted in various areas of the
Successor Agency and Housing Successor Agency budgets.
The Administrative Budget for the period of July 1, 2021 through June 30, 2022 totals
$393,916. These funds will be included in various line items in Program 20 of Fund 460
in the fiscal year 2021-22 budget and are included on the Recognized Obligation
Payment Schedule (ROPS).
Staff recommends approval of the ROPS 21-22 and administrative budget by adopting
Resolution No. SA 2021-001 and SA 2021-002.

FISCAL IMPACT
The California State Department of Finance and the Oversight Board must approve
the ROPS and administrative budget for the City to be able to expend the funds as
proposed. Funds are sufficiently budgeted in the annual operation budget.

STRATEGIC PLAN

  WHEREAS, The Community Redevelopment Agency of the City of Palmdale
(“Redevelopment Agency”) was a redevelopment agency in the City of Palmdale
(“City”), duly created pursuant to the California Community Redevelopment Law (Part 1
(commencing with SECTION 33000) of Division 24 of the California Health and Safety
Code) (“Redevelopment Law”); and

  WHEREAS, The City Council has adopted redevelopment plans for Palmdale’s
redevelopment project areas, and from time to time, the City Council has amended such
redevelopment plans; and

  WHEREAS, The Redevelopment Agency was responsible for the administration
of redevelopment activities within the City; and

  WHEREAS, Assembly Bill 1X 26 (“AB 26”) was signed by the Governor on June
28, 2011 and upheld to be constitutional by the California Supreme Court on December
29, 2011; and

  WHEREAS, AB 26 made certain changes to the California Community
Redevelopment Law (Part 1 (commencing with SECTION 33000) of Division 24 of the
California Health and Safety Code), including adding Part 1.8 (commencing with
SECTION 34161) and Part 1.85 (commencing with SECTION 34170) (“Part 1.85”) to
Division 24 of the California Health and Safety Code (“Health and Safety Code”); and

  WHEREAS, On February 1, 2012, as a result of the Supreme Court’s decision,
all California redevelopment agencies were dissolved, successor agencies were
established as successor agencies to the former redevelopment agencies pursuant to
Health and Safety Code SECTION 34173, and successor agencies are tasked with
paying, performing and enforcing the enforceable obligations of the former
redevelopment agencies and winding down the affairs of the former redevelopment
agencies; and

  WHEREAS, On June 27, 2012 the Governor of California signed Assembly Bill
1484 (“AB 1484”) into law, making several substantive and technical amendments to AB
26 (AB 26 and AB 1484 together referred to as the “Dissolution Bills”); and

  WHEREAS, On January 4, 2012 the City Council adopted Resolution No. CC
2012-002 declaring itself as the Successor Agency to the Community Redevelopment
Agency of the City of Palmdale (“Successor Agency”) upon the dissolution of the
Redevelopment Agency; and

  WHEREAS, On April 4, 2012 the City Council, acting in its capacity as the
Successor Agency, adopted Resolution No. CC 2012-041 SA naming itself the
“Successor Agency to the Community Redevelopment Agency of the City of Palmdale”,
the sole name by which it will exercise its powers and fulfill its duties pursuant to Part
1.85 of AB 26, and establishing itself as a separate legal entity with rules and
regulations that will apply to the governance and operations of the Successor Agency;
and

  WHEREAS, pursuant to Health and Safety Code Section 34179 (q), commencing
on and after July 1, 2018, the County of Los Angeles, where more than 40 oversight
boards were created by the Dissolution Act, shall have five consolidated oversight
boards each encompassing the five supervisorial districts; and

  WHEREAS, the Fifth Supervisorial District Consolidated Oversight Board ("Fifth
District Consolidated Oversight Board") has jurisdiction over the Successor Agency of
the Former Redevelopment Agency to the City of Palmdale; and

  WHEREAS, the Fifth District Consolidated  Oversight  Board  held  a
regular/special meeting on January 14, 2021; and

  WHEREAS, Health & Safety Code SECTION 34177(l) (“SECTION 34177(l)”)
requires the Successor Agency to prepare, a forward looking Recognized Obligation
Payment Schedule (ROPS) listing the enforceable obligations of the former
Redevelopment Agency that are due in the next annual period; and

  WHEREAS, SECTION 34177(l), as amended by AB 1484, also provides that (i)
the ROPS shall be submitted to the county administrative officer, the Los Angeles
County Auditor-Controller (“Auditor-Controller”) and the State Department of Finance
(“Department of Finance”) at the same time that the Successor Agency submits the
ROPS to the Los Angeles County Fifth Supervisorial District Consolidated Oversight
Board for approval; (ii) the ROPS shall be submitted to and duly approved by the Los
Angeles County Fifth Supervisorial District Consolidated Oversight Board; (iii) the
approved ROPS shall be posted on the Successor Agency’s website; and (iv) the
approved ROPS shall be submitted to the Auditor Controller, the State Controller and
the State Department of Finance; and

  WHEREAS, Health & Safety Code SECTION 34179.7 (o) (1), requires the
Successor Agency to prepare a forward looking, annual Recognized Obligation
Payment Schedule (ROPS) listing the enforceable obligations of the former
Redevelopment Agency that are due in the next annual period and submitting an

  APPROVING THE ADMINISTRATIVE BUDGET FOR THE PERIOD OF
  JULY 1, 2021 THROUGH JUNE 30, 2022 (ADMINISTRATIVE BUDGET
  21-22)

  WHEREAS, The Community Redevelopment Agency of the City of Palmdale
(“Redevelopment Agency”) was a redevelopment agency in the City of Palmdale
(“City”), duly created pursuant to the California Community Redevelopment Law
(Part 1 (commencing with Section 33000) of Division 24 of the California Health and
Safety Code) (“Redevelopment Law”); and

  WHEREAS, The City Council has adopted redevelopment plans for
Palmdale’s redevelopment project areas, and from time to time, the City Council has
amended such redevelopment plans; and

  WHEREAS, The Redevelopment Agency was responsible  for  the
administration of redevelopment activities within the City; and

  WHEREAS, Assembly Bill 1X 26 (“AB 26”) was signed by the Governor on
June 28, 2011 and upheld to be constitutional by the California Supreme Court on
December 29, 2011; and

  WHEREAS, AB 26 made certain changes to the California Community
Redevelopment Law (Part 1 (commencing with Section 33000) of Division 24 of the
California Health and Safety Code), including adding Part 1.8 (commencing with
Section 34161) and Part 1.85 (commencing with Section 34170) (“Part 1.85”) to
Division 24 of the California Health and Safety Code (“Health and Safety Code”); and

  WHEREAS, On February 1, 2012, as a result of the Supreme Court’s
decision, all California redevelopment agencies were dissolved, successor agencies
were established as successor agencies to the former redevelopment agencies
pursuant to Health and Safety Code Section 34173, and successor agencies are
tasked with paying, performing and enforcing the enforceable obligations of the

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council adopt Resolution No. CC 2021-001, continuing

BACKGROUND
ln December 2019, a new communicable disease, Coronavirus Disease (COVID-19), was
first detected in Wuhan City, Hubei Province, China. Since that time, it has spread globally
to over 122 countries, infecting more than 126,000 individuals and resulting in more than
4,614 deaths. Symptoms of the virus include fever, cough, and shortness of breath, and
infected individuals have experienced a range of outcomes, from mild sickness to severe
illness and death. This incident is being called the “COVID-19 outbreak.”

On January 31, 2020, the United States Secretary of Health and Human Services, Alex
M. Azar ll, declared a Public Health Emergency to aid the United States in responding to
COVID-19. This order was renewed on April 26, 2020.

On March 4, 2020, the State of California declared a State of Emergency to aid in the
prevention and mitigation of the effects of the COVID-19 outbreak. That same day, the
County of Los Angeles declared a State of Emergency to prevent the further spread of
COVID-19 throughout the County of Los Angeles. Since that time, the counties of Orange,
Santa Clara, San Diego, Sonoma, and San Francisco, along with the cities of Los
Angeles, Long Beach, and San Francisco have also declared local health emergencies.

Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19), Resolution No. CC 2020-048 and authorizing the
Director of Emergency Services to continue to take appropriate measures to protect the
public health, safety, and welfare, and obtain emergency aid from other agencies.

The City Council adopted Resolution No. CC 2020-049 on April 7, 2020 and continued
the state of emergency.

On June 2, 2020, the City Council adopted Resolution No. CC 2020-057 continuing the
proclamation of a local emergency.

proclamation of a local emergency.

On October 6, 2020, the City Council adopted Resolution No. CC 2020-104 continuing
the proclamation of a local emergency.

On November 17, 2020, the City Council adopted Resolution No. CC 2020-110 continuing
the proclamation of a local emergency.

The local emergency will continue until terminated by the City Council. The City Council’s
ratification of the local emergency is valid for sixty (60) days, unless extended by further
City Council action.

of a Local Emergency resulting from Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19).

Subida Avenue on to City Ranch Road into the Waste Management site. The project
consisted of street improvements. The public improvements have been installed per the
approved construction plan, inspected and approved by City Public Works inspection
staff.

completed to the satisfaction of the City Engineer as required in the
Subdivision/Development Improvement Agreement between the developer and the City.

one-year period, thereafter transferring maintenance responsibility of these
improvements from the developer, to the City of Palmdale. This council action will also

DISCUSSION

BACKGROUND
In August 2020, the City awarded a contract with Deark E & C to provide for American
with Disabilities Act (ADA) improvements to the Palmdale Transportation Center. Exterior
site work included restriping affected areas of ADA parking stalls, installation of
delineators and international symbol of accessibility markings, access striping and
signage. Truncated domes, accessible ramps and detectable directional texture would
be added to the train platform at the Metrolink openings. Inside the building, a wall
between the female restroom and the utility closet would be demolished and rebuilt with
enough clearance to provide a wheelchair turning radius within the female ADA stall.
Other small ADA improvement would be conducted in the lobby area.

DISCUSSION
In 2019, the initial project budget was $300,000. The project was awarded to Deark E&C,
Inc. for $167,700. The scope of Supplemental Agreement No. 1 includes the adjustment
of the wall between the female restroom and the utility room, the removal, cutting, and
reinstallation of the female restroom countertop, and additional site curb ramp
replacement at two locations and a portion of sidewalk replacement.

The wall between the restroom and utility room was assumed to include 4” studs but field
conditions revealed to show 6” studs. This required additional structural calculations and
redesign, as the floor drain would also need to be relocated. Additionally, the female
restroom sink was noted to be located too high to meet ADA clearance and the contractor
was directed to lower the sink countertop. Upon lowering the countertop, the sink apron
did not allow for the minimum 27” knee clearance below the sink. It was determined that
the countertop would need to be removed, the sink apron cut, and the countertop
reinstalled to meet all appropriate ADA clearances.

In association with sitework, the original scope of work included work along one defined
path of travel from the accessible parking to the bus depot and the train station and
building. After meeting with Building and Safety and the City Attorney’s office, it was
determined that to address the PTC ADA issues more comprehensively, additional ADA
upgrades to secondary and tertiary paths of travel would be beneficial to the City,
especially in avoiding future ADA liability issues. This additional work includes a portion
of sidewalk that needs to be replaced and two additional curb cut replacements.

FISCAL IMPACT
Sufficient funds exist in the PTC ADA Upgrade Account B0004203 for the additional
cost of Supplemental Agreement No. 1 of $42,566.

DATE:  JANUARY 12, 2021

SUBJECT:  ADOPT ORDINANCE NO. 1557 ADDING CHAPTER 2.60
  “ELECTRONIC SIGNATURES” TO THE PALMDALE MUNICIPAL
  CODE AUTHORIZING THE USE OF ELECTRONIC AND DIGITAL
  SIGNATURES BY THE CITY

ISSUE
Ordinance No. 1557 adding Chapter 2.60 (“Electronic Signatures”) to the Palmdale
Municipal Code authorizing the use of electronic and digital signatures by the City.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Receive public testimony regarding Proposed Ordinance No. 1557; and
  2. Adopt Ordinance No. 1557.

BACKGROUND
For several years, the City has taken steps, and made a significant investment, towards
improving and modernizing its business practices. Part of that effort is moving towards
a “paperless” office. To help facilitate these efforts, the City should embrace the use of
electronic and digital signatures on those documents that require signatures.

For years, state and federal law have authorized the use of electronic and digital
signatures. California has approved the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (“UETA”),
which authorizes the use of electronic signatures and provides that such signatures
have the same legal effect as traditional signatures. Electronic signatures were granted
similar treatment on the federal level though the passage of the Electronic Signatures in
Global and National Commerce Act. California also allows, pursuant to California
Government Code §16.5, public entities to accept digital signatures so long as these
signatures comply with certain regulations to ensure that the signature is unique and
verifiable to the user.

The use of electronic and digital signatures has certain advantages, including, but not
limited to, reduction in the cost and time associated with the transmission of records,
reduction in the use of paper products, and reduction in the time associated with

has become increasingly prevalent in recent years. The recent COVID-19 pandemic

importance.

DISCUSSION
Proposed Ordinance No. 1557 would specifically authorize the City to use electronic and
digital signatures by adding Chapter 2.60 to the Palmdale Municipal Code. This Chapter
would require that the use of such signatures be in compliance with state laws and
regulations designed to ensure the veracity of the signature.

transmission of records, reduction in the use of paper products, and reduction in the
time associated with processing records; and
